cards.r: さるもきからおちる
cards.mean: even an expert sometimes makes a mistake
cards.lit: even monkeys, the best of climbers, sometimes fall out of trees

use.how: Quoted whole, often with だ, だね or って言う, about a skilled person's slip; often said to comfort them or to excuse the mistake. Never about beginners.

near.diff: Same idea, but more bookish and about a master of a craft; 猿も木から落ちる is the everyday, lighter version.

cards.cue: The office spreadsheet wizard, who never gets anything wrong, sends round a file with a broken formula, and everyone teases them kindly.

ctx.en: "So even you, who are always perfect, make mistakes. Don't worry about it. Even monkeys fall out of trees, as they say."

bad.en: (meant: I fell over a lot on my first day skiing)

bad.why: It is not about general unpredictability; it is only about an expert making a mistake. For an uncertain future, use issun saki wa yami.

cards.r: いそがばまわれ
cards.mean: the safe, longer route gets you there sooner than a risky shortcut
cards.lit: if you are in a hurry, go the long way round

story.text: The saying is traced to a waka attributed to the renga poet Sōchō: the boat from Yabase is fast, but if you are in a hurry, go round by the long bridge at Seta. Travellers heading for Kyoto could save distance by crossing Lake Biwa by boat, but sudden winds off Mount Hiei often held the boats up or put them in danger, so the long road over the Seta bridge was the surer way.
story.source: Waka attributed to the renga poet Sōchō (宗長), on Lake Biwa

use.how: Quoted whole as advice or as a reason, often with だ, で or って言う, for choosing the steady, safe method over a risky shortcut.

near.t: 急いては事を仕損じる
near.diff: 急いては事を仕損じる warns that rushing causes mistakes; 急がば回れ adds that the longer, safer way actually gets you there sooner.

cards.cue: A colleague wants to skip testing so the app ships faster; you point out that the careful route will actually get it finished sooner.

ctx.s: 「その近道[ちかみち]は細[ほそ]くて迷[まよ]いやすいよ。{急[いそ]がば回[まわ]れ}で、大通[おおどお]りを行[い]こう。」
ctx.en: "That shortcut is narrow and easy to get lost on. More haste, less speed: let's take the main road."

ctx.s: 基礎[きそ]を飛[と]ばして応用問題[おうようもんだい]ばかり解[と]いても伸[の]びない。{急[いそ]がば回[まわ]れ}だ。

cards.r: ななころびやおき

use.how: Used as a noun or motto: 七転び八起きの人生, 七転び八起きの精神, 七転び八起きだよ. Praises or encourages someone who keeps trying after many setbacks.

near.diff: 石の上にも三年 is about patiently enduring one hard situation; 七転び八起き is about getting back up after many separate failures.
失敗は成功のもと says failure teaches you how to succeed; 七転び八起き says keep standing up again, however many times you fall.

cards.lit: sit even on a cold stone for three years and it grows warm

near.diff: 七転び八起き is about getting up after many failures; 石の上にも三年 is about patiently staying put through one hard stretch.

cards.t: 塵も積もれば山となる
cards.r: ちりもつもればやまとなる
cards.mean: tiny amounts, piled up over time, become something big
cards.lit: even specks of dust, if they pile up, become a mountain

use.how: Quoted whole, often with だ or で, about saving small sums or doing a little every day; also as a warning that small wastes add up. Often shortened to 塵も積もれば.

near.diff: 千里の道も一歩から is about making the first small step of a big task; 塵も積もれば山となる is about small amounts adding up over time.

cards.r: ひゃくぶんはいっけんにしかず
cards.mean: seeing something once beats hearing about it a hundred times
cards.lit: hearing a hundred times does not equal seeing once

story.text: Under the Han dynasty, the Qiang peoples rose in revolt on the western frontier. Emperor Xuan asked the veteran general Zhao Chongguo, then over seventy, how the rising should be handled and how many troops he would need. Zhao answered that hearing a hundred times is not as good as seeing once: a campaign is hard to judge from far away, so he asked to ride to the frontier himself and draw up his plan there.
story.source: 『漢書』趙充国伝 (Book of Han, biography of Zhao Chongguo)

cards.r: そなえあればうれいなし
cards.mean: if you are prepared, you have nothing to worry about
cards.lit: if there is preparation, there is no worry

story.text: The saying goes back to the Chinese classic the Book of Documents. In the chapter in which the minister Fu Yue advises King Wu Ding of Shang, he says that every undertaking needs its preparation, and that where there is preparation there is nothing to fear. Its four-character phrase, read the Japanese way, became this proverb.

cards.r: たなからぼたもち

ctx.en: My senior got transferred and the role came to me. It just fell into my lap.

ctx.en: I went to help a friend move and got all the furniture they didn't need. A real windfall.

ctx.s: 「{棚[たな]からぼたもち}なんて、そうそうあるもんじゃないよ。」

bad.en: (meant: after three years of daily practice, we finally won)

bad.s: 急[きゅう]に仕事[しごと]を押[お]し付[つ]けられて、{棚[たな]からぼたもち}だよ。
bad.en: (meant: extra work was dumped on me out of the blue)

cards.r: てつはあついうちにうて
cards.mean: strike while conditions are ripe, or teach people while they are young
cards.lit: strike the iron while it is still hot

story.text: The saying is the Japanese rendering of the European proverb 'Strike while the iron is hot', taken from the blacksmith's forge: iron can be shaped only while it is red-hot, and once it cools the chance is gone. In Japanese it is used both for seizing a favourable moment and, very often, for training people while they are young and receptive.
story.source: European proverb, 'Strike while the iron is hot'

use.how: Advice to act while momentum or openness lasts, especially to teach the young or newcomers early: 鉄は熱いうちに打てで、新人のうちに基本を教える。

near.diff: 善は急げ says do a good thing at once; 鉄は熱いうちに打て says act while conditions or a person's receptiveness last, often about training.

cards.cue: Your nephew has suddenly become excited about the piano, and his mother books lessons this week before the enthusiasm fades.

ctx.s: 勝[か]って勢[いきお]いがある今[いま]のうちに、次[つぎ]の目標[もくひょう]を決[き]めよう。{鉄[てつ]は熱[あつ]いうちに打[う]て}だ。
ctx.en: Let's set our next goal now, while we have the momentum from winning. Strike while the iron is hot.

ctx.s: 新入社員[しんにゅうしゃいん]には、最初[さいしょ]のうちに基本[きほん]をしっかり教[おし]えよう。{鉄[てつ]は熱[あつ]いうちに打[う]て}だ。
ctx.en: Let's teach the new staff the basics properly right at the start. Strike while the iron is hot.

ctx.s: 「息子[むすこ]さんが興味[きょうみ]を持[も]っている今[いま]のうちに、色々[いろいろ]教[おし]えてあげたら？{鉄[てつ]は熱[あつ]いうちに打[う]て}って言[い]うし。」
ctx.en: "Why not teach your son all sorts of things now, while he's interested? Strike while the iron is hot, as they say."

ctx.s: 語学[ごがく]の勉強[べんきょう]も{鉄[てつ]は熱[あつ]いうちに打[う]て}で、若[わか]いうちに始[はじ]めたほうがいい。
ctx.en: Learning a language is no different: strike while the iron is hot and start while you're young.

ctx.s: 監督[かんとく]は「{鉄[てつ]は熱[あつ]いうちに打[う]て}だ」と言[い]って、一年生[いちねんせい]に毎日[まいにち]基礎[きそ]練習[れんしゅう]をさせた。
ctx.en: Saying you have to strike while the iron is hot, the coach had the first-years do basic drills every day.

bad.s: 腹[はら]が立[た]ったら、{鉄[てつ]は熱[あつ]いうちに打[う]て}で、すぐ相手[あいて]に文句[もんく]を言[い]おう。
bad.en: (meant: when you're angry, complain at once while you're still angry)
bad.why: 'Hot' means ripe conditions or a young, receptive mind, not acting in the heat of anger.

bad.s: ラーメンは{鉄[てつ]は熱[あつ]いうちに打[う]て}だから、早[はや]く食[た]べて。
bad.en: (meant: eat the ramen while it's hot)
bad.why: It is not about eating food hot. For that say samenai uchi ni tabete.

cards.t: 人は見かけによらぬもの
cards.r: ひとはみかけによらぬもの
cards.mean: you cannot judge what a person is like from how they look
cards.lit: a person is not as their looks would suggest

use.how: A comment on finding a person different from how they look, usually better (a fierce face, a gentle heart), sometimes worse. In speech often 人は見かけによらない.

cards.cue: The tattooed, scary-looking man next door turns out to run a free reading club for the neighbourhood children.

ctx.s: あの強面[こわもて]の店長[てんちょう]、実[じつ]は猫[ねこ]が大好[だいす]きなんだって。{人[ひと]は見[み]かけによらない}ね。
ctx.en: That tough-looking manager is apparently crazy about cats. You can't judge people by their looks.

ctx.s: おとなしそうな彼女[かのじょ]が、ボクシングのチャンピオンだとは。{人[ひと]は見[み]かけによらぬもの}だ。
ctx.en: Who'd have thought that gentle-looking woman was a boxing champion? People are not what they seem.

ctx.s: 「あの人[ひと]、真面目[まじめ]そうなのに遅刻[ちこく]ばっかりなんだよ。」「{人[ひと]は見[み]かけによらない}もんだね。」
ctx.en: "He looks so conscientious, but he's late all the time." "Goes to show you can't tell from looks."

ctx.s: 「あの派手[はで]な格好[かっこう]の学生[がくせい]、学年[がくねん]で一番[いちばん]成績[せいせき]がいいんだって。」「へえ、{人[ひと]は見[み]かけによらない}なあ。」

ctx.s: 面接[めんせつ]では、{人[ひと]は見[み]かけによらぬもの}だと思[おも]って、服装[ふくそう]だけで判断[はんだん]しないようにしている。
ctx.en: In interviews I remind myself that looks can deceive, and try not to judge candidates by their clothes alone.

ctx.en: The boy who seemed so rough was kinder than anyone. A person is not what he appears to be.

bad.s: 第一印象[だいいちいんしょう]が大事[だいじ]だから、{人[ひと]は見[み]かけによらぬもの}で、面接[めんせつ]にはスーツを着[き]ていこう。
bad.en: (meant: first impressions matter, so wear a suit to the interview)

bad.s: 優[やさ]しそうな顔[かお]の先生[せんせい]は、やっぱり優[やさ]しかった。{人[ひと]は見[み]かけによらぬもの}だ。
bad.en: (meant: the kind-looking teacher was kind, just as I thought)
bad.why: It is said only when a person turns out different from their looks, not when looks and nature match.

cards.t: 案ずるより産むが易し
cards.r: あんずるよりうむがやすし
cards.mean: something you dread turns out easier once you actually do it
cards.lit: giving birth is easier than all the worrying about it beforehand

use.how: Said to encourage someone nervous before a task (大丈夫、案ずるより産むが易しだよ), or afterwards on finding it went smoothly: やってみたら案ずるより産むが易しだった。

ctx.en: I was nervous about my first solo trip, but it turned out far easier than I feared, and I loved it.

ctx.s: 「スピーチ、緊張[きんちょう]するなあ。」「大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]、{案[あん]ずるより産[う]むが易[やす]し}だよ。」
ctx.en: "I'm so nervous about the speech." "You'll be fine. It's never as hard as you fear."

ctx.s: 英語[えいご]で電話[でんわ]するのは怖[こわ]かったが、かけてみたら{案[あん]ずるより産[う]むが易[やす]し}だった。
ctx.en: I was scared of making a phone call in English, but once I did it, it was much easier than I'd feared.

ctx.en: Resistance to the new system had been expected, but it went far more smoothly than feared, with almost no confusion.

bad.s: 心配[しんぱい]していた通[とお]り、試験[しけん]は本当[ほんとう]に難[むずか]しかった。{案[あん]ずるより産[う]むが易[やす]し}だ。
bad.en: (meant: the exam was as hard as I'd feared)
bad.why: It is used only when the thing turns out easier than feared, never when the fear proves right.

bad.s: このケーキは材料[ざいりょう]を混[ま]ぜて焼[や]くだけなので、{案[あん]ずるより産[う]むが易[やす]し}だ。

cards.t: 好きこそ物の上手なれ
cards.r: すきこそもののじょうずなれ
cards.mean: you become good at what you love doing
cards.lit: it is liking a thing, above all, that makes you skilled at it

use.how: Said about someone who got good at something because they love it, often a hobby or a child's passion: 好きこそ物の上手なれで、絵がうまくなった。

ctx.en: My brother loved video games so much that, as they say, love makes you skilled: now he's a pro.

ctx.en: "Your cooking has got really good." "I enjoy cooking every day. You get good at what you love."

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]の日本語[にほんご]が上手[じょうず]なのは、アニメが好[す]きだからだろう。{好[す]きこそ物[もの]の上手[じょうず]なれ}だ。
ctx.en: Her Japanese is probably so good because she loves anime. Love is the best teacher.

ctx.en: "How can I get better at guitar?" "You get good at what you love. Start by enjoying it."

ctx.en: Rather than forcing my children, I want to nurture what they enjoy. They say love is what makes you skilled.

ctx.s: 勉強[べんきょう]は苦手[にがて]だった彼[かれ]も、虫[むし]のことになると誰[だれ]よりも詳[くわ]しい。{好[す]きこそ物[もの]の上手[じょうず]なれ}である。
ctx.en: He was never good at school, yet when it comes to insects he knows more than anyone. One excels at what one loves.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]はピアノが嫌[きら]いなのに、とても上手[じょうず]だ。{好[す]きこそ物[もの]の上手[じょうず]なれ}だね。
bad.en: (meant: he hates the piano yet plays it very well)
bad.why: The proverb says skill grows from love of the activity, so it contradicts a case of skill without liking.

bad.s: 苦手[にがて]でも、{好[す]きこそ物[もの]の上手[じょうず]なれ}だから我慢[がまん]して練習[れんしゅう]しなさい。
bad.en: (meant: even if you dislike it, grit your teeth and practise)
bad.why: Nare here is classical (after koso), not an order. The saying credits liking a thing for skill, so it cannot urge enduring what you dislike.

cards.r: ほとけのかおもさんどまで
cards.mean: even the most patient person gets angry if wronged again and again
cards.lit: even the Buddha's face, only up to three times: if you stroke it a third time, even he gets angry

near.diff: 二度あることは三度ある predicts that a thing will happen a third time; 仏の顔も三度まで warns that another offence will exhaust patience.

cards.cue: Your roommate has twice taken your car without asking and you let it go; now they've done it again, and you tell them this is the last time.

ctx.s: 今[いま]までの遅刻[ちこく]は許[ゆる]してきたけど、{仏[ほとけ]の顔[かお]も三度[さんど]まで}だよ。
ctx.en: I've let your lateness go so far, but my patience has its limits.

ctx.s: 「また約束[やくそく]を破[やぶ]ったの？{仏[ほとけ]の顔[かお]も三度[さんど]まで}だからね。」
ctx.en: "You broke your promise again? Even a saint runs out of patience, you know."

ctx.s: いつも優[やさ]しい部長[ぶちょう]が、同[おな]じミスを繰[く]り返[かえ]す部下[ぶか]をついに叱[しか]った。{仏[ほとけ]の顔[かお]も三度[さんど]まで}だ。
ctx.en: Our ever-gentle manager finally scolded the employee who kept making the same mistake. Even the patient have their limits.

ctx.en: They say even the Buddha's patience lasts only three times, and my mother's finally ran out too.

ctx.s: 無断[むだん]キャンセルが続[つづ]いた客[きゃく]に、店主[てんしゅ]は「{仏[ほとけ]の顔[かお]も三度[さんど]まで}です」と予約[よやく]を断[ことわ]った。
ctx.en: To a customer who kept cancelling without notice, the owner said his patience had run out and refused the booking.

ctx.s: 隣[となり]の騒音[そうおん]には何度[なんど]も目[め]をつぶってきたが、{仏[ほとけ]の顔[かお]も三度[さんど]}、今回[こんかい]は苦情[くじょう]を言[い]うことにした。
ctx.en: I'd turned a blind eye to the neighbours' noise many times, but patience has limits, and this time I decided to complain.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は何[なに]をされても怒[おこ]らない。{仏[ほとけ]の顔[かお]も三度[さんど]まで}のような人[ひと]だ。
bad.en: (meant: he never gets angry, he's as patient as a Buddha)
bad.why: It says that patience runs out, not that someone is endlessly patient. For that, say hotoke no you na hito.

bad.s: 二回[にかい]落[お]ちたけど、{仏[ほとけ]の顔[かお]も三度[さんど]まで}だから次[つぎ]はきっと合格[ごうかく]できる。
bad.en: (meant: I failed twice, so third time lucky, I'll pass)
bad.why: That is sando-me no shoujiki. This proverb is about someone's patience running out after repeated wrongs.

cards.r: ふくすいぼんにかえらず
cards.mean: what is done, or a relationship that is broken, cannot be undone
cards.lit: spilled water does not go back into the basin

story.text: Lü Shang (Taigong Wang) was so poor and so absorbed in study that his wife left him. Later he rose to high office, and she came back asking to be his wife again. He poured a basin of water onto the ground and told her to put it back. When she could not, he told her that a couple once parted cannot come together again, just as spilled water cannot return to the basin.
story.source: 《拾遺記》, the tale of Lü Shang (太公望)

use.how: Said of a word, act or broken relationship that cannot be taken back, as a warning or a sober verdict: 一度言ったことは覆水盆に返らずだ。

near.diff: 後悔先に立たず warns that regret comes too late; 覆水盆に返らず states flatly that what is done, or a broken bond, cannot be restored.

cards.cue: Years after walking out on her husband, a woman asks to come back to him, and he quietly answers that it is far too late.

ctx.s: 一度[いちど]言[い]ってしまった言葉[ことば]は取[と]り消[け]せない。{覆水[ふくすい]盆[ぼん]に返[かえ]らず}だ。
ctx.en: Words once spoken can't be taken back. What's done is done.

ctx.s: 誤[あやま]って送[おく]ったメールはもう取[と]り消[け]せない。{覆水[ふくすい]盆[ぼん]に返[かえ]らず}と諦[あきら]めて、相手[あいて]におわびの連絡[れんらく]をした。
ctx.en: The email I sent by mistake couldn't be recalled. Accepting that what's done is done, I contacted the recipient to apologise.

ctx.s: 「今[いま]さら謝[あやま]っても、{覆水[ふくすい]盆[ぼん]に返[かえ]らず}じゃない？」
ctx.en: "Apologising now isn't going to undo it, is it?"

bad.en: (meant: I broke a plate but glued it back together)

cards.t: 背に腹は代えられない

bad.en: (meant: I love this job, so nothing could replace it)

bad.en: (meant: I won the lottery, so I'm over the moon)
bad.why: It is said when need forces a reluctant sacrifice, never about good fortune or happiness.

cards.r: なきっつらにはち
cards.mean: a fresh misfortune hitting someone who is already suffering
cards.lit: a bee stinging a face that is already crying

use.how: A predicate noun: まさに泣きっ面に蜂だ, or 泣きっ面に蜂の思い. Said, often wryly, of bad luck landing on top of bad luck.

cards.r: いっすんさきはやみ
cards.mean: no one can know what will happen even in the near future
cards.lit: one sun (about three centimetres) ahead, it is pitch dark

use.how: Said as a statement about life or a field: 人生は一寸先は闇だ, 勝負の世界は一寸先は闇. A sober warning that sudden trouble can come at any moment.

ctx.en: Someone who was fine yesterday suddenly in hospital: none of us knows what tomorrow holds.

ctx.en: Show business is said to be a world where anything can happen at any moment.

bad.en: (meant: the fog is so thick I can't see ahead to drive)

bad.why: The darkness is ominous: it warns of sudden misfortune and never expresses cheerful anticipation.

cards.t: 郷に入っては郷に従え
cards.r: ごうにいってはごうにしたがえ
cards.mean: follow the customs of the place you are in
cards.lit: when you enter a village, obey the village

cards.r: しっぱいはせいこうのもと
cards.mean: failure teaches what you need to succeed next time
cards.lit: failure is the source of success

bad.en: (meant: I scolded my subordinate harshly for a costly mistake)

cards.t: 二兎を追う者は一兎をも得ず
cards.r: にとをおうものはいっとをもえず
cards.mean: chase two goals at once and you end up with neither
cards.lit: whoever chases two hares catches not even one

story.text: This saying came into Japanese as a translation of a European proverb, known in English as 'If you run after two hares, you will catch neither.' The image is of a hunter who tries to catch two hares at once and ends up catching neither.
story.source: European proverb: 'If you run after two hares, you will catch neither'

near.diff: 一石二鳥 is gaining two things from one action; 二兎を追う者は一兎をも得ず warns that pursuing two aims at once wins neither.

cards.r: せんりのみちもいっぽから
cards.mean: even a huge undertaking starts with one small step
cards.lit: even a road of a thousand ri begins with a single step

story.text: The Daodejing, the classic attributed to Laozi, says that a tree so big it takes both arms to circle grows from a tiny shoot, a tower of nine storeys rises from a heap of earth, and a journey of a thousand li begins beneath your feet. The Japanese proverb is traced to this last line. A thousand li simply means a very long way.

near.t: 塵も積もれば山となる
near.diff: 塵も積もれば山となる is about small amounts adding up over time; 千里の道も一歩から is about taking the first step toward a big goal.

ctx.en: Every journey starts with a single step. Let's begin today by opening the textbook at page one.

ctx.en: "There's no way I can tidy the whole house." "One step at a time. Let's just do one drawer today."

ctx.en: The president told the new recruits, "Every long road starts with one step. Don't rush; learn the basics first."

ctx.en: It is when facing a big goal that I want to remember the saying that every long journey begins with one step.

cards.t: 井の中の蛙大海を知らず

near.t: 船頭多くして船山に上る
near.diff: That saying is the opposite warning: with too many people giving orders, a project goes wrong. 三人寄れば文殊の知恵 praises thinking together.

cards.cue: Three classmates stuck on a group project, none of them an expert, decide that if they brainstorm together they will surely think of something.

ctx.s: 一人[ひとり]で悩[なや]まないで、みんなで考[かんが]えようよ。{三人[さんにん]寄[よ]れば文殊[もんじゅ]の知恵[ちえ]}って言[い]うじゃない。
ctx.en: Don't agonise over it alone; let's all think about it together. Two heads are better than one, as they say.

ctx.s: 難[むずか]しい問題[もんだい]も、友達[ともだち]と相談[そうだん]したら解[と]けた。まさに{三人[さんにん]寄[よ]れば文殊[もんじゅ]の知恵[ちえ]}だ。
ctx.en: Even that hard problem got solved once I talked it over with my friends. Two heads really are better than one.

ctx.s: 「{三人[さんにん]寄[よ]れば文殊[もんじゅ]の知恵[ちえ]}だね。こんないい案[あん]が出[で]るとは思[おも]わなかった！」
ctx.en: "Put our heads together and look at that! I never thought we'd come up with such a good idea!"

ctx.s: 専門家[せんもんか]がいなくても、{三人[さんにん]寄[よ]れば文殊[もんじゅ]の知恵[ちえ]}で何[なん]とかなるんじゃないかな。
ctx.en: Even without an expert, if we put our heads together we can probably manage, can't we?

ctx.s: 予算[よさん]が足[た]りず困[こま]っていたが、{三人[さんにん]寄[よ]れば文殊[もんじゅ]の知恵[ちえ]}で、チームは新[あたら]しい方法[ほうほう]を見[み]つけた。
ctx.en: Short of budget, the team was stuck, but by pooling their ideas they found a new way forward.

ctx.s: {三人[さんにん]寄[よ]れば文殊[もんじゅ]の知恵[ちえ]}と申[もう]しますように、本日[ほんじつ]は皆様[みなさま]の自由[じゆう]なご意見[いけん]をお聞[き]かせください。
ctx.en: As the saying goes, many minds make good ideas, so today please share your views freely.

bad.s: 会議[かいぎ]に人[ひと]が多[おお]すぎて、{三人[さんにん]寄[よ]れば文殊[もんじゅ]の知恵[ちえ]}で何[なに]も決[き]まらなかった。
bad.en: (meant: there were too many people at the meeting, so nothing got decided)
bad.why: It says that gathering produces good ideas; too many voices causing confusion calls for the opposite saying about too many boatmen.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は一人[ひとり]で何[なん]でも解決[かいけつ]できる、{三人[さんにん]寄[よ]れば文殊[もんじゅ]の知恵[ちえ]}のような人[ひと]だ。
bad.en: (meant: he is so clever he can solve anything on his own)
bad.why: It is about the wisdom of a group of ordinary people, not praise for one person's brilliance.

cards.r: いしばしをたたいてわたる
cards.mean: to be extremely careful, checking even what is surely safe
cards.lit: to tap a stone bridge, which is surely solid, before walking across it

use.how: Verb phrase about a careful person or way of acting: 彼は石橋を叩いて渡るタイプだ。 Can be approving or gently teasing about overcaution.

near.diff: 転ばぬ先の杖 is preparing in advance against trouble; 石橋を叩いて渡る is checking again and again before acting, even when it already seems safe.

cards.cue: Before signing for a flat that is plainly fine, your friend has it inspected twice, reads every clause and phones the previous tenant.

ctx.s: 何度[なんど]も確認[かくにん]するなんて、君[きみ]は本当[ほんとう]に{石橋[いしばし]を叩[たた]いて渡[わた]る}タイプだね。
ctx.en: Checking it that many times? You really are the type who never takes a step without testing the ground.

ctx.s: 父[ちち]は{石橋[いしばし]を叩[たた]いて渡[わた]る}性格[せいかく]で、買[か]い物[もの]でも何日[なんにち]も比[くら]べる。
ctx.en: My father is extremely cautious by nature; even when shopping he compares things for days.

ctx.s: そこまで{石橋[いしばし]を叩[たた]いて渡[わた]らなくても}、もう大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]じゃない？
ctx.en: You don't have to be that careful, surely it's fine by now?

ctx.s: 「新[あたら]しい取引先[とりひきさき]とは、{石橋[いしばし]を叩[たた]いて渡[わた]る}くらいでちょうどいい」と部長[ぶちょう]は言[い]った。
ctx.en: "With a new client, being overly careful is just about right," said the department head.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は{石橋[いしばし]を叩[たた]いて渡[わた]る}ように、契約書[けいやくしょ]を一行[いちぎょう]ずつ確[たし]かめた。
ctx.en: Leaving nothing to chance, she checked the contract line by line.

ctx.s: その会社[かいしゃ]は{石橋[いしばし]を叩[たた]いて渡[わた]る}慎重[しんちょう]な経営[けいえい]で、不況[ふきょう]を乗[の]り越[こ]えた。
ctx.en: The company came through the recession thanks to its extremely cautious management.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は危険[きけん]を恐[おそ]れず、{石橋[いしばし]を叩[たた]いて渡[わた]る}冒険家[ぼうけんか]だ。
bad.en: (meant: he is a fearless adventurer who takes risks)
bad.why: It means extreme caution, the very opposite of a bold risk-taker.

bad.s: 試験[しけん]の前[まえ]に、{石橋[いしばし]を叩[たた]いて渡[わた]る}ように一生懸命[いっしょうけんめい]勉強[べんきょう]した。
bad.en: (meant: I studied very hard before the exam)
bad.why: It is about caution and double-checking before acting, not about hard work or effort.

cards.r: かえるのこはかえる
cards.mean: a child grows up to be like its parents
cards.lit: the child of a frog is a frog: a tadpole looks nothing like its parents, yet grows into a frog

use.how: A comment on a child who turned out like a parent in ability, job or habits: 蛙の子は蛙で、息子も教師になった。 Often said modestly of one's own family.

near.diff: 鳶が鷹を生む is the opposite case: ordinary parents have an exceptional child. 蛙の子は蛙 says the child is just like the parents.
三つ子の魂百まで is about one's own early-childhood character lasting; 蛙の子は蛙 compares a child with its parents.

cards.cue: Both your parents are teachers. You swore you would do something else, and now you stand in front of a class every morning too.

ctx.s: 娘[むすめ]も私[わたし]と同[おな]じで朝[あさ]が苦手[にがて]だ。{蛙[かえる]の子[こ]は蛙[かえる]}だなあ。
ctx.en: My daughter is bad at mornings, just like me. Like parent, like child.

ctx.s: 両親[りょうしん]とも医者[いしゃ]で、彼[かれ]も医者[いしゃ]になった。{蛙[かえる]の子[こ]は蛙[かえる]}というわけだ。
ctx.en: Both his parents are doctors, and he became one too. The apple didn't fall far from the tree.

ctx.s: 「うちの子[こ]には無理[むり]ですよ。{蛙[かえる]の子[こ]は蛙[かえる]}ですから」と母親[ははおや]は笑[わら]った。
ctx.en: "Oh, my child could never do that. He takes after us," the mother laughed.

ctx.s: 歌手[かしゅ]の娘[むすめ]さんがデビューしたらしい。やっぱり{蛙[かえる]の子[こ]は蛙[かえる]}なのかな。
ctx.en: Apparently the singer's daughter has made her debut. I suppose children really do follow their parents.

ctx.s: 店[みせ]を継[つ]がないと言[い]っていた息子[むすこ]が、結局[けっきょく]パン屋[や]になった。{蛙[かえる]の子[こ]は蛙[かえる]}だね。
ctx.en: The son who said he'd never take over the shop ended up a baker after all. Like father, like son.

ctx.s: 祖父[そふ]も父[ちち]も短気[たんき]だったが、私[わたし]もすぐ怒[おこ]る。{蛙[かえる]の子[こ]は蛙[かえる]}とはよく言[い]ったものだ。
ctx.en: My grandfather and father were both short-tempered, and I lose my temper easily too. How true it is that children take after their parents.

bad.s: 平凡[へいぼん]な両親[りょうしん]から天才[てんさい]が生[う]まれた。まさに{蛙[かえる]の子[こ]は蛙[かえる]}だ。
bad.en: (meant: ordinary parents had a genius child)
bad.why: That is the opposite case, a hawk born to a kite (tonbi ga taka o umu); this saying means the child turned out like the parents.

bad.s: 小[ちい]さい頃[ころ]の性格[せいかく]は大人[おとな]になっても変[か]わらない。{蛙[かえる]の子[こ]は蛙[かえる]}だ。
bad.en: (meant: the character you have as a small child never changes)
bad.why: It compares a child with its parents; for one's own childhood character lasting, the saying is mitsugo no tamashii hyaku made.

cards.r: おににかなぼう
cards.mean: something that makes the already strong even stronger
cards.lit: an iron club for an oni, an ogre who is already strong

use.how: Usually 〜があれば鬼に金棒だ: about something added to a person, team or business that is already strong.

cards.cue: The football team already top of the league has just signed the best striker in the country.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は英語[えいご]も得意[とくい]だから、中国語[ちゅうごくご]まで話[はな]せたら{鬼[おに]に金棒[かなぼう]}だね。
ctx.en: He's already good at English, so if he can speak Chinese too, he'll be unbeatable.

ctx.s: 「優勝候補[ゆうしょうこうほ]のチームにあの選手[せんしゅ]が入[はい]ったよ。」「それは{鬼[おに]に金棒[かなぼう]}だな。」
ctx.en: "That player has joined the title favourites." "Now they'll be even more formidable."

ctx.s: 料理上手[りょうりじょうず]な母[はは]が新[あたら]しいオーブンを買[か]って、まさに{鬼[おに]に金棒[かなぼう]}だ。
ctx.en: My mother, already a great cook, has bought a new oven. Now there's no stopping her.

ctx.s: 経験豊富[けいけんほうふ]なあなたが資格[しかく]も取[と]れば、{鬼[おに]に金棒[かなぼう]}じゃないですか。
ctx.en: With all your experience, if you get the qualification as well, won't you be unstoppable?

ctx.s: もともと成績[せいせき]のいい弟[おとうと]に家庭教師[かていきょうし]までついて、{鬼[おに]に金棒[かなぼう]}となった。
ctx.en: My brother already had good grades, and now he has a private tutor as well, making him stronger still.

ctx.s: 技術力[ぎじゅつりょく]のある企業[きぎょう]が豊富[ほうふ]な資金[しきん]を得[え]たことは、{鬼[おに]に金棒[かなぼう]}と言[い]える。
ctx.en: A technically strong company gaining plentiful funding can be said to have become stronger than ever.

bad.s: 何[なに]もできない私[わたし]に新[あたら]しいパソコンを買[か]ってもらって、{鬼[おに]に金棒[かなぼう]}だ。
bad.en: (meant: a new computer is a big help to me, though I can't do anything)
bad.why: It needs someone already strong; help given to someone who says they can do nothing is not an iron club for an ogre.

bad.s: 部長[ぶちょう]は怖[こわ]い顔[かお]でいつも怒鳴[どな]る、{鬼[おに]に金棒[かなぼう]}のような人[ひと]だ。
bad.en: (meant: the boss is a scary man who is always shouting)
bad.why: It is not about being frightening or harsh; it means a strength made even greater by something added.

cards.r: こういんやのごとし
cards.mean: time passes as swiftly as an arrow flies
cards.lit: light and shadow, days and nights, go by like an arrow

use.how: A complete remark looking back on how fast months or years have gone, typical of speeches, letters and reflective talk: 光陰矢の如しで、もう十年だ。

near.diff: 時は金なり says time is valuable, so do not waste it; 光陰矢の如し marvels at how fast time has already gone by.

cards.cue: At a twentieth class reunion, the former class president stands up and says graduation feels like yesterday.

ctx.s: もう年末[ねんまつ]か。{光陰矢[こういんや]の如[ごと]し}だね。
ctx.en: The end of the year already? Time really flies.

ctx.s: {光陰矢[こういんや]の如[ごと]し}で、娘[むすめ]ももう大学生[だいがくせい]になりました。
ctx.en: Time flies: my daughter is already at university.

ctx.s: 留学[りゅうがく]してもう一年[いちねん]？{光陰矢[こういんや]の如[ごと]し}だなあ。
ctx.en: It's already a year since you went abroad to study? How time flies.

ctx.s: 「{光陰矢[こういんや]の如[ごと]し}と申[もう]しますが、皆[みな]さんと過[す]ごした三年間[さんねんかん]はあっという間[ま]でした。」
ctx.en: "They say time flies like an arrow, and the three years I spent with you all went by in a flash."

ctx.s: 退職[たいしょく]の挨拶[あいさつ]で、彼[かれ]は「{光陰矢[こういんや]の如[ごと]し}とはよく言[い]ったものです」と語[かた]った。
ctx.en: In his retirement speech he said, "How true it is that time flies like an arrow."

ctx.s: {光陰矢[こういんや]の如[ごと]し}、あの日[ひ]からもう五年[ごねん]が経[た]ちましたね。
ctx.en: Time flies; five years have already passed since that day, haven't they?

bad.s: 彼[かれ]の走[はし]るスピードは{光陰矢[こういんや]の如[ごと]し}だ。
bad.en: (meant: he runs as fast as an arrow)
bad.why: It is only about time passing quickly, never about the speed of a person or a thing.

bad.s: 今日[きょう]の会議[かいぎ]は十分[じゅっぷん]で終[お]わった。{光陰矢[こういんや]の如[ごと]し}だ。
bad.en: (meant: today's meeting was short, only ten minutes)
bad.why: It marvels at months or years slipping by; a meeting that simply did not last long is not time flying.

cards.r: やけいしにみず
cards.mean: help so small it makes no difference to a big problem
cards.lit: water on a red-hot stone: a few drops hiss away and the stone stays hot

use.how: Predicate about a measure or amount set against a big problem, often after では or 〜ても: この程度の節約では焼け石に水だ。

cards.cue: Your company is losing millions a year, and management's answer is to switch off the office lights at lunchtime.

ctx.s: この暑[あつ]さでは、小[ちい]さな扇風機[せんぷうき]なんて{焼[や]け石[いし]に水[みず]}だ。
ctx.en: In this heat, a little fan is a drop in the ocean.

ctx.s: 百万円[ひゃくまんえん]も借金[しゃっきん]があるのに、一万円[いちまんえん]返[かえ]しても{焼[や]け石[いし]に水[みず]}だよ。
ctx.en: You owe a million yen; paying back ten thousand won't make a dent.

ctx.s: 「アルバイトを増[ふ]やそうか。」「この人手不足[ひとでぶそく]じゃ、二人[ふたり]増[ふ]やしても{焼[や]け石[いし]に水[みず]}だよ。」

ctx.en: Studying for just one hour the night before the exam won't do much good, will it?

ctx.s: 赤字[あかじ]があまりに大[おお]きく、多少[たしょう]の経費削減[けいひさくげん]では{焼[や]け石[いし]に水[みず]}だった。
ctx.en: The deficit was so large that a few spending cuts made no real difference.

ctx.s: 寄付[きふ]は集[あつ]まったが、修理[しゅうり]に必要[ひつよう]な額[がく]には遠[とお]く、{焼[や]け石[いし]に水[みず]}の状態[じょうたい]だ。
ctx.en: Donations have come in, but they are far from what the repairs need: a drop in the bucket.

bad.s: 熱[ねつ]があったので、{焼[や]け石[いし]に水[みず]}で冷[つめ]たいタオルを当[あ]てたら楽[らく]になった。
bad.en: (meant: I had a fever, and a cold towel cooled me down and helped)

bad.s: 突然[とつぜん]の転勤[てんきん]の話[はなし]は、私[わたし]にとって{焼[や]け石[いし]に水[みず]}だった。
bad.en: (meant: the sudden news of my transfer came as a complete shock)
bad.why: That confuses it with nemimi ni mizu; this saying is about help too small to matter, not about a surprise.

cards.r: ねみみにみず
cards.mean: shocking news that comes with no warning at all
cards.lit: water poured into your ear while you are asleep

use.how: Usually 〜は寝耳に水だった or 寝耳に水の話: about startling, usually unwelcome news that came with no warning.

near.diff: 藪から棒 describes someone saying or doing something abruptly; 寝耳に水 describes the shock of hearing news you had no inkling of.

cards.cue: You arrive at work on Monday and learn from a notice on the door that your branch closes at the end of the month.

ctx.s: 「来月[らいげつ]から家賃[やちん]が上[あ]がるって知[し]ってた？」「え、{寝耳[ねみみ]に水[みず]}だよ。」
ctx.en: "Did you know the rent goes up next month?" "What? That's the first I've heard of it!"

ctx.s: 会社[かいしゃ]の合併[がっぺい]は、社員[しゃいん]にとって{寝耳[ねみみ]に水[みず]}の話[はなし]だった。
ctx.en: The company merger came as a bolt from the blue to the employees.

ctx.s: 担任[たんにん]の先生[せんせい]が辞[や]めるなんて、{寝耳[ねみみ]に水[みず]}で驚[おどろ]いた。
ctx.en: I was stunned to hear our homeroom teacher was leaving; nobody had said a word.

ctx.s: 長年[ながねん]通[かよ]った店[みせ]が閉店[へいてん]すると聞[き]いて、{寝耳[ねみみ]に水[みず]}で言葉[ことば]を失[うしな]った。
ctx.en: When I heard that the shop I'd gone to for years was closing, it came out of nowhere and I was lost for words.

ctx.s: 取引先[とりひきさき]からの契約打[けいやくう]ち切[き]りの連絡[れんらく]は、まさに{寝耳[ねみみ]に水[みず]}でした。
ctx.en: The client's notice that they were ending the contract came completely out of the blue.

ctx.s: 本人[ほんにん]にとっては{寝耳[ねみみ]に水[みず]}だったかもしれないが、噂[うわさ]は前[まえ]からあった。
ctx.en: It may have come as a total shock to him, but there had been rumours for a while.

bad.s: 宝[たから]くじが当[あ]たって、{寝耳[ねみみ]に水[みず]}でとても嬉[うれ]しかった。
bad.en: (meant: I won the lottery and was thrilled by the surprise)
bad.why: It is used for startling, usually unwelcome news; a happy windfall out of nowhere is tana kara botamochi.

bad.s: 被害[ひがい]が大[おお]きすぎて、少[すこ]しの寄付[きふ]では{寝耳[ねみみ]に水[みず]}だ。
bad.en: (meant: the damage is so great that a small donation won't help)
bad.why: That confuses it with yakeishi ni mizu; this saying is about news that comes as a shock, not about too little help.

cards.r: りょうやくはくちににがし
cards.mean: good advice, like good medicine, is unpleasant to take
cards.lit: good medicine tastes bitter in the mouth

story.text: In the Kongzi Jiayu (The School Sayings of Confucius), Confucius says that good medicine is bitter in the mouth but benefits the illness, and that loyal advice grates on the ear but benefits one's conduct. The Japanese proverb keeps the first half; the advice it stands for is the second.
story.source: 《孔子家語》 (Kongzi Jiayu)

use.how: Quoted to accept or justify harsh but useful criticism: 良薬は口に苦しと言うから、彼の意見を聞こう。 Said by the one receiving it, or to soften one's own criticism.

cards.cue: Your editor tears your first chapter apart. It stings, but you realise every point would make the book better.

ctx.s: 先輩[せんぱい]の注意[ちゅうい]は厳[きび]しいけど、{良薬[りょうやく]は口[くち]に苦[にが]し}だと思[おも]って聞[き]いている。
ctx.en: My senior's criticism is harsh, but I listen, telling myself that what's good for you is hard to swallow.

ctx.s: 「部長[ぶちょう]にかなり厳[きび]しく言[い]われたよ。」「{良薬[りょうやく]は口[くち]に苦[にが]し}って言[い]うじゃない。」
ctx.en: "The boss gave me a real dressing-down." "Well, good advice is bitter medicine, as they say."

ctx.s: コーチの言葉[ことば]は痛[いた]かったが、{良薬[りょうやく]は口[くち]に苦[にが]し}で、おかげで試合[しあい]に勝[か]てた。
ctx.en: The coach's words hurt, but they were the bitter medicine I needed, and thanks to them we won the match.

ctx.s: 友人[ゆうじん]は「{良薬[りょうやく]は口[くち]に苦[にが]し}だから、はっきり言[い]うね」と言[い]って、私[わたし]の欠点[けってん]を挙[あ]げた。
ctx.en: Saying "The truth hurts, but it's good for you, so I'll be blunt," my friend listed my faults.

ctx.s: 耳[みみ]の痛[いた]い意見[いけん]こそ大切[たいせつ]にしたい。{良薬[りょうやく]は口[くち]に苦[にが]し}と言[い]うではないか。
ctx.en: It's the opinions that are hard to hear that we should value most. Isn't good medicine always bitter?

ctx.s: お客様[きゃくさま]からの厳[きび]しい評価[ひょうか]も、{良薬[りょうやく]は口[くち]に苦[にが]し}と受[う]け止[と]め、改善[かいぜん]に生[い]かしてまいります。
ctx.en: We take even our customers' harsh reviews as bitter but useful medicine and will put them to use in improving.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は口[くち]が悪[わる]くて、いつも人[ひと]の悪口[わるくち]ばかり言[い]う。{良薬[りょうやく]は口[くち]に苦[にが]し}だ。
bad.en: (meant: he has a nasty tongue and is always bad-mouthing people)

cards.r: あたまかくしてしりかくさず
cards.mean: thinking you have hidden something when much of it still shows

cards.t: 火のない所に煙は立たぬ

cards.r: いちをきいてじゅうをしる
cards.mean: so quick-witted that a hint is enough to grasp everything
cards.lit: to hear one and understand ten

story.text: In the Analects, Confucius asks his disciple Zigong who is the better of the two, Zigong or Yan Hui. Zigong answers that he cannot compare himself with Yan Hui: when Yan Hui hears one thing he understands ten, while Zigong hears one thing and understands only two. Confucius agrees that Zigong is not his equal.

ctx.en: Yan Hui, a disciple of Confucius, is said to have been so brilliant that he heard one thing and understood ten.

cards.r: こうぼうふでをえらばず

story.text: Kōbō Daishi is the posthumous title of Kūkai, the early Heian-period monk who founded the Shingon school of Japanese Buddhism. use.how: Quoted whole, often with だ or って言う, to say skill matters more than equipment: to someone who blames their tools, or in admiration of an expert.

near.diff: 弘法にも筆の誤り says even a master sometimes makes mistakes; 弘法筆を選ばず says a master works well with any tools.

cards.r: にんげんばんじさいおうがうま
cards.mean: good and bad fortune cannot be predicted and often trade places
cards.lit: in human life, everything is like the old frontier man's horse

story.text: An old man living by a frontier fortress lost his horse when it ran off into nomad lands; when neighbours pitied him, he said it might be good luck. cards.t: 虎穴に入らずんば虎子を得ず
cards.r: こけつにいらずんばこじをえず
cards.mean: you cannot win something great without taking a great risk
cards.lit: if you do not go into the tiger's den, you cannot get the tiger's cub

story.text: When the Han envoy Ban Chao reached the kingdom of Shanshan, the king's warm welcome suddenly cooled: envoys of the Xiongnu had arrived. cards.r: とらのいをかるきつね

story.text: A tiger caught a fox, and the fox said: Heaven has made me king of the beasts, so eating me would defy Heaven; walk behind me and see. cards.r: きゅうそねこをかむ

cards.r: わざわいてんじてふくとなす
cards.mean: to turn a misfortune into something good

story.text: When the state of Qi seized ten cities from Yan, the strategist Su Qin went to the king of Qi and persuaded him to give them back, arguing that the wise turn misfortune into fortune and failure into success. 雨降って地固まる is a relationship made stronger after a quarrel; 災い転じて福となす is any misfortune turned into a gain.

cards.lit: putting a lid on something that stinks

use.how: Used with だ or の, or as 臭いものに蓋をする, to criticise covering up a problem or scandal instead of fixing it: 臭いものに蓋の対応だ。

near.diff: 頭隠して尻隠さず mocks a clumsy cover-up that leaves things showing; 臭いものに蓋 criticises hiding the problem at all instead of solving it.

cards.cue: A school learns a teacher has been bullying pupils and quietly moves the teacher to another school instead of investigating.

ctx.s: 問題[もんだい]を隠[かく]しても解決[かいけつ]しないよ。{臭[くさ]いものに蓋[ふた]}じゃだめだ。
ctx.en: Hiding the problem won't solve it. Just covering it up is no good.

ctx.s: 散[ち]らかった物[もの]をクローゼットに押[お]し込[こ]むのは、{臭[くさ]いものに蓋[ふた]をする}だけだよ。
ctx.en: Shoving all the mess into the wardrobe is just putting a lid on it.

ctx.s: 「データの不正[ふせい]を公表[こうひょう]しないなんて、{臭[くさ]いものに蓋[ふた]をする}つもりですか」
ctx.en: "You're not going to make the falsified data public? Are you planning to just cover it up?"

ctx.s: 家族[かぞく]の借金[しゃっきん]の話[はなし]をずっと避[さ]けてきたが、{臭[くさ]いものに蓋[ふた]をして}も何[なに]も変[か]わらないと気[き]づいた。
ctx.en: I'd always avoided talking about the family's debts, but I realised that covering it up wouldn't change anything.

ctx.s: 学校[がっこう]はいじめの事実[じじつ]を認[みと]めず、{臭[くさ]いものに蓋[ふた]}の対応[たいおう]に終始[しゅうし]した。
ctx.en: The school refused to admit the bullying and did nothing but try to hush it up.

ctx.s: {臭[くさ]いものに蓋[ふた]をする}体質[たいしつ]を改[あらた]めない限[かぎ]り、同[おな]じ不祥事[ふしょうじ]は繰[く]り返[かえ]される。
ctx.en: Unless the organisation changes its culture of hushing things up, the same scandals will keep happening.

bad.s: 生[なま]ゴミの臭[にお]いがひどいので、ゴミ箱[ばこ]に{臭[くさ]いものに蓋[ふた]をした}。
bad.en: (meant: the kitchen scraps smelled awful, so I put the lid on the bin)
bad.why: It is a figurative criticism of covering up problems; for a real bin you simply say you put the lid on.

bad.s: 友達[ともだち]の失敗[しっぱい]を誰[だれ]にも言[い]わないであげるなんて、{臭[くさ]いものに蓋[ふた]をする}優[やさ]しい人[ひと]だね。
bad.en: (meant: you kindly kept your friend's mistake to yourself, how sweet)
bad.why: It criticises evading a problem; it cannot praise kind discretion, and it would make the friend's mistake sound like a stinking scandal.

cards.r: しょしんわするべからず
cards.mean: never lose the fresh resolve you had as a beginner
cards.lit: you must not forget the beginner's mind

story.text: The Noh master Zeami wrote these words in his treatise on acting, Kakyō (1424). He meant that a performer should never forget how unskilled he was at the start, and should keep in mind the beginner's stage of every period of his career, even in old age. Today it is mostly used to mean keeping the enthusiasm and resolve one had at the start.
story.source: 世阿弥『花鏡』 (Zeami, Kakyō)

use.how: Quoted as a full sentence or with の気持ち, as a motto or reminder, often to newcomers or to people grown used to their work or success: 初心忘るべからずですね。

cards.cue: Ten years after opening her ramen shop, the owner still rereads the notebook where she wrote her goals on the first day.

ctx.s: 机[つくえ]の前[まえ]に「{初心[しょしん]忘[わす]るべからず}」と書[か]いた紙[かみ]を貼[は]っている。
ctx.en: I've stuck a sheet of paper saying "Never forget your beginner's spirit" above my desk.

ctx.s: 仕事[しごと]に慣[な]れてきた頃[ころ]こそ、{初心[しょしん]忘[わす]るべからず}だよ。
ctx.en: It's just when you're getting used to the job that you need to remember how you felt at the start.

ctx.s: 「十年目[じゅうねんめ]でも毎朝[まいあさ]自分[じぶん]で店[みせ]を掃除[そうじ]するんですね」「{初心[しょしん]忘[わす]るべからず}ですから」
ctx.en: "Ten years in and you still clean the shop yourself every morning?" "Well, you should never forget where you started."

ctx.s: 入社式[にゅうしゃしき]で社長[しゃちょう]は、新入社員[しんにゅうしゃいん]に「{初心[しょしん]忘[わす]るべからず}」という言葉[ことば]を贈[おく]った。
ctx.en: At the welcome ceremony, the president gave the new employees the words: never lose the spirit you start with.

ctx.s: 優勝[ゆうしょう]しても浮[う]かれず、{初心[しょしん]忘[わす]るべからず}の気持[きも]ちで練習[れんしゅう]を続[つづ]けたい。
ctx.en: Even after winning, I don't want to get carried away; I want to keep training with the same spirit I had as a beginner.

ctx.s: ベテランになるほど自己流[じこりゅう]に陥[おちい]りやすい。{初心[しょしん]忘[わす]るべからず}という世阿弥[ぜあみ]の言葉[ことば]は、今[いま]も重[おも]い。
ctx.en: The more experienced you get, the easier it is to slip into your own bad habits. Zeami's words about never forgetting the beginner's mind still carry weight.

bad.s: 明日[あした]は試験[しけん]だから、{初心[しょしん]忘[わす]るべからず}で鉛筆[えんぴつ]を持[も]っていこう。
bad.en: (meant: the exam is tomorrow, so don't forget to bring pencils)
bad.why: It is about keeping one's original attitude and resolve, not about remembering things to take with you.

bad.en: (meant: I still remember my first love)
